Those trade-offs are business decisions and they will be made either explicitly now or implicitly by me later, and explicit is better. I would write the resulting numbers into the requirements with the stakeholder's name against them, so the design has an agreed basis rather than my assumptions.

rubric.guidance: Convert adjectives into measurable targets.
Translate availability into downtime and cost.
Time to first token and realistic peak load.
Surface trade-offs as business decisions and record them.

prompt: Why should an LLM provider be placed behind an abstraction, and what belongs in that abstraction?
modelAnswer: Because you will change providers. A price change, an outage, a compliance decision, or simply a newer model that is better at your task will force it, and if provider SDK types appear throughout your orchestration code then each change is a migration project rather than a configuration change. The abstraction should expose the common surface: messages with roles, a system instruction, temperature and max tokens, tool definitions, streaming, and — importantly — token usage on every response, because cost tracking bolted on later costs three times as much effort. Keep it narrow: an abstraction exposing every provider-specific option is not an abstraction. Where providers genuinely differ, the adapter normalises: Anthropic takes the system prompt as a top-level parameter while OpenAI treats it as a message, tool-call shapes differ, and token counting differs. That normalisation is the value the adapter adds. The abstraction is also the right place for resilience — retry with exponential backoff honouring Retry-After, and circuit breaking — with one important detail: retry only 429 and 5xx, because retrying a 400 just repeats the same malformed request three times at the same cost.

rubric.guidance: You will change providers; make it a config change.
What the interface exposes, including token usage.
The adapter's job is normalising real differences.
Retry only what is worth retrying.

prompt: What distinguishes an agent from a workflow, and which should be the default?
modelAnswer: A workflow has a path decided at design time: the model may fill in steps, but the sequence is yours. An agent decides its own path at runtime, choosing which tools to call and when to stop. The default should be the workflow, and the test is simple: can you draw the flowchart? If you can, build the flowchart. It is deterministic, testable, cheap and produces a stack trace when it breaks. Most problems described as needing an agent are workflows — 'read the email, classify it, look up the customer, draft a reply' is a fixed sequence. An agent is justified when the next step genuinely depends on what the last one found: open-ended investigation, troubleshooting where each finding changes the next question, or tasks where the number of steps depends on what is discovered. The costs are real and worth stating: an eight-step agent means eight inferences plus eight tool round trips, latency in seconds to minutes, cost per task ten to fifty times a single call, and debugging that means reconstructing a non-deterministic trace. All acceptable when the flexibility is genuinely needed, and indefensible when it is not.

rubric.guidance: Who decides the path, and when.
The flowchart test and the workflow default.
Genuine agent cases.
Quantify the cost of choosing an agent.

prompt: Leadership wants an AI feature live in six weeks. Your honest estimate is sixteen. How do you handle it?
scenario: The feature is a customer-facing assistant over product documentation. The six-week date is tied to a conference announcement.
modelAnswer: I would neither agree to six weeks nor simply refuse. The productive move is to separate the deadline from the scope and offer options with their consequences. First, understand what the six weeks is really for: a conference announcement means they need something demonstrable, which is not the same as production-ready for all customers. That distinction often resolves the whole conversation. Then present options honestly. Option one: a limited pilot in six weeks — one product area, internal users or a small customer cohort, read-only, with human review — which is genuinely deliverable and gives them something real to announce. Option two: the full scope in sixteen weeks. Option three: full scope in six weeks with named cuts — no evaluation harness, no permission model beyond authentication, no cost controls — and I would state plainly what each cut means, because 'no evaluation' means quality regressions reach customers undetected and 'no permission model' may mean a customer sees another customer's documentation. For a customer-facing feature I would say directly that option three is not one I would recommend, and why. Then let them decide; the scope-versus-date trade is a business decision, not mine. What I would not do is agree and then miss, or agree and quietly cut the safety work — both destroy credibility, and the second one destroys it at the worst possible moment. I would also put the options in writing so the decision is recorded.

rubric.guidance: Understand what the date is actually for.
Offer real options with their consequences.
Name what is lost and give a recommendation.
Let the business decide; record it.

prompt: Design a system that migrates an on-premises .NET monolith to Azure while adding AI capability, without a big-bang rewrite.
scenario: Fifteen-year-old ASP.NET application, SQL Server, 300 tables, 200 internal users, business-critical. Leadership wants cloud and AI within a year.
modelAnswer: A big-bang rewrite of a fifteen-year-old business-critical system is how these projects fail, so I would not propose one. The approach is the strangler fig: new capability goes to new services while the monolith keeps running, and functionality migrates incrementally behind a routing layer. Sequence. First, lift and shift to Azure with minimal change — the application onto App Service or VMs, SQL Server to Azure SQL Managed Instance, which tolerates legacy features that Azure SQL Database does not. This gets you to the cloud without changing the application and buys time. Second, put a gateway in front so requests can be routed per-endpoint to either the monolith or a new service; without this, incremental migration is not possible. Third, add the AI capability as a new service from the start rather than inside the monolith. This is the important sequencing insight: AI is new functionality, so there is no legacy to migrate and no reason to put it where it will be hard to change. It can call the monolith's data through an API or a read replica. Fourth, migrate functionality outward in order of value and independence, starting with something read-heavy and low-risk to prove the pattern. Data is the hard part: 300 tables means shared data is everywhere, so I would use read models and replication rather than trying to split the database early, and split it only where a service genuinely needs write ownership. Risks to name: dual running costs during migration, team capacity while also keeping the existing system alive, and the temptation to let 'temporary' routing become permanent. I would define success as functionality migrated and release independence achieved, not as a date for the monolith's retirement — and I would be explicit that some of it may never move, which is an acceptable outcome.

rubric.guidance: Strangler fig with a routing layer, not a rewrite.
A staged sequence starting with low-change migration.
AI as new capability outside the monolith — the key insight.
Data is the hard part; avoid an early database split.
Name the risks honestly, including partial migration.

prompt: Why must an evaluation set include questions the system cannot answer?
modelAnswer: Because refusing correctly is a feature with its own failure mode, and you cannot measure it with answerable questions alone. If every case in the evaluation set has an answer in the corpus, a system that always answers scores perfectly — including one that invents an answer whenever retrieval fails. Unanswerable questions are the only way to distinguish 'knows the answer' from 'always produces an answer'. In an enterprise setting that distinction is the whole point: a confident wrong answer about a policy is far worse than a clean 'I could not find that in the available documents', because the user acts on it. Practically I would include three kinds of unanswerable case: questions about topics genuinely outside the corpus, questions where a near-miss document exists that a weak system would latch onto, and questions where the corpus contains related but insufficient information — which is the hardest case and the most common in reality. Then measure refusal accuracy alongside groundedness and recall, and tune the relevance threshold against it, because that threshold is the dial between too many refusals and too many wrong answers.

rubric.guidance: Without them you cannot detect a system that always answers.
A confident wrong answer is worse than a refusal.
Include near-miss and insufficient-information cases.
Use it to tune the relevance threshold.

prompt: Design a multi-region deployment for an AI application with a 99.99% availability target.
scenario: Customer-facing AI assistant. Global users. Azure. Data residency allows EU and US regions but data must not cross between them.
modelAnswer: 99.99% is about four minutes of downtime a month, which means no manual intervention is possible — recovery must be automatic. I would first push back gently and establish what an outage actually costs, because the step from 99.9% to 99.99% multiplies cost substantially and is sometimes not warranted. Assuming it is: residency rules out a single global data plane, so this is two independent regional stacks rather than one stack spanning regions. Each region has its own compute, its own data stores, its own model deployments and its own search index; users are routed to their region by Front Door using geographic routing, and data never crosses. That also means a regional failure cannot fail over to the other region for EU users — which must be stated explicitly, because it caps what availability can mean. Within each region: multi-zone deployment for compute and data, zone-redundant configurations for Azure SQL and storage, and at least two model deployments so a single deployment's quota or availability problem is not a regional outage. Health probes must check dependencies rather than returning 200 unconditionally, because a service that is up but cannot reach its search index should be taken out of rotation. Automatic recovery: circuit breakers, retries with jitter, and a defined degraded mode — if the model is unavailable, return retrieved documents without a generated answer rather than failing entirely, which keeps the feature partially useful. Deployment safety matters as much as infrastructure at this tier: revision-based traffic shifting with automatic rollback on error rate, because most outages are caused by deployments, not hardware. I would also insist on testing failure deliberately — a zone failure and a model deployment failure exercised on a schedule — since an untested failover is an assumption rather than a control.

rubric.guidance: Translate 99.99% into what it demands and question whether it is warranted.
Residency means independent stacks and caps failover options.
Zone redundancy and multiple model deployments.
Degraded mode, safe deployment and tested failover.

prompt: Users report that the assistant gives different answers to the same question. Investigate.
scenario: Internal policy assistant. Same question asked twice within minutes returns materially different answers.
modelAnswer: Several causes, and I would check them in order of likelihood. Temperature: if it is above roughly 0.2, sampling variation alone will produce different phrasing and sometimes different substance. For a factual assistant this should be near zero, and it is the most common cause. Retrieval non-determinism: approximate nearest-neighbour search can return slightly different candidate sets between calls, and if the relevance threshold sits near the boundary, one call includes a document the other excludes — which changes the answer materially rather than cosmetically. I would log the retrieved document IDs per request; if they differ between the two calls, the cause is retrieval rather than generation. Conversation context: if the two questions were asked in different sessions, or one had prior turns, the context differs even though the question looks identical. Load balancing across model deployments or regions, where versions may differ subtly. And provider-side failover, if the gateway silently routed to a secondary provider — which is why recording the provider per request matters. Remediation depends on cause, but I would set temperature near zero for factual answering, make retrieval deterministic enough by fixing candidate counts and reviewing the threshold, pin model versions across deployments, and log retrieved documents, model, version and provider on every request so the next report takes minutes rather than a day. Some variation in phrasing is inherent and acceptable; variation in substance is a defect, and distinguishing the two is the first thing I would establish with the users.

rubric.guidance: The most common cause.
Approximate search near a threshold — the insightful answer.
Context differences, version skew, silent failover.
Log what is needed and distinguish phrasing from substance.

prompt: How do you decide when a system is 'good enough' to ship?
modelAnswer: By agreeing the bar before building, not after. For any system I want three things defined up front: the functional criteria, the non-functional targets with numbers, and the explicit list of what is deliberately not being done in this release. 'Good enough' is then a measurement rather than a judgement call under deadline pressure, which is when judgement is worst. For AI systems specifically the bar needs quality criteria that most teams omit: a groundedness or accuracy threshold on an evaluation set, refusal accuracy, and a latency and cost budget. Without those, 'it seems to work in the demo' becomes the bar by default. I also distinguish between what must be right before shipping and what can be learned in production. Security, data protection and irreversible actions must be right before — those have no safe learning path. Retrieval tuning, prompt refinement and coverage can improve after launch, provided you have the measurement to know whether they are improving. That distinction lets you ship earlier without shipping recklessly. And I think shipping to a limited audience first is almost always right for AI features, because real usage reveals failure modes that no evaluation set anticipates. A pilot with fifty users for two weeks is not a delay; it is the cheapest way to find out what you got wrong.

rubric.guidance: The bar is agreed before building.
Quality thresholds specific to AI.
Distinguish what cannot be learned in production.
Limited release as a discovery mechanism.
